note: Vol. I No. 7, and the issue that carries the town's own ordinances. The Board of Trustees met at Dexter Graves's house on 4 December 1833 and passed, among others, the wharfing clause that reserves eighty feet of street along the Chicago River — which is the most consequential single sentence this reading pass has found. The ordinance column is set THROUGH the Chicago Academy's advertisement on the same lines, so five of these claims use character spans inside one 1,378-character line and each of them quotes the Academy's book list along with the ordinance; that is recorded in every claim rather than smoothed away.

That is a building doing the town's public business six weeks after the town incorporated, and the reconstruction can say whose house it was. Everything in claims c002 to c005 was passed at this sitting, and this claim is what dates and places them. Graves's tavern is independently in this same issue as a landmark other advertisers navigate by ('nearly opposite Graves' Tavern', claim c008), so the house and the tavern are almost certainly one building; the identification is NOT asserted here, because the ordinance says 'the house of' and the advertisement says 'Tavern' and nothing in this issue joins them.

claims.notes: THE TOWN'S FIRST SURVEYOR, NAMED AND PRICED: George W. Snow, assessor and surveyor of the town of Chicago from 4 December 1833, at three dollars a day. Every street line, every lot corner and every assessment the corporation made in its first year passed through this man, which makes him the single most consequential name in the ordinance for a project whose whole subject is where things stood. He is also the 'G. W. Snow' who signs as clerk pro tem of the Board in the ordinance of 6 June 1834 already in this corpus (1834-07-02, claim c017), and the same name appears in the county election returns of August 1834 — one man across eight months of the town's administration. The initials 'Geo[rge] [W.]' are supplied from those later printings and bracketed; this line prints 'Geo RR AY Snow'.

claims.notes: THE WHARFING PRIVILEGE, AND EIGHTY FEET FOR A STREET. This is the legal instrument behind the whole South Water Street river frontage, passed 4 December 1833: an owner whose lot fronts the Chicago River may occupy the vacant ground between his lot and the water — but must LEAVE EIGHTY FEET FOR A STREET — and pays fifteen dollars a year in advance to the Treasurer for the privilege. Three separate things the reconstruction has had to decide are answered here by an ordinance rather than by inference: that the ground between the lots and the river was OCCUPIED by the abutters and not public open ground; that a street width of EIGHTY FEET was reserved along it by law; and that the arrangement was a paid, annual, revocable privilege rather than ownership. The wharf layer (T-0059) and every question about what stands between South Water Street and the water begin here. THE FIGURE IS THE POINT AND IT IS NOT SUPPLIED: 'leaving vighty feot for a atreef' is legible as eighty feet, and the fifteen dollars is legible as printed. What is NOT read is the rest of clause 15's conditions and clause 16, which continue past this line's end into text the column does not preserve.

claims.notes: THE TOWN CONTRACTS FOR BRIDGES ON BOTH BRANCHES, 4 DECEMBER 1833. The plural is in the print — 'the Bridges on the North and South' — so the Board is authorising more than one, and it is authorising them at the moment of incorporation rather than years later. For a reconstruction standing eighteen months downstream of this ordinance, it dates the intent that produced the crossings a visitor walks over. WHAT IS NOT CLAIMED: the word after 'South' is lost, so 'branches' is a supply from the sense of 'the North and South' in a town with two of them; and nothing here says a bridge was BUILT, only that the Trustees ordered a contract made for building them.

claims.notes: THE CORPORATION'S FIRST ATTORNEY: J. Dean Caton, appointed 4 December 1833 for one year. He is in this corpus already as half of Collins & Caton, whose office the issue of 1834-01-28 places 'at [the] door east of Brewster, Hogan & Co.' and whose advertising runs through 1834 — so the town's lawyer and a South Water Street storefront are the same man, and the professional class of this town is small enough that the corporation hired from it. The given name is printed only as 'Dean Caton' here and the 'J.' is supplied from his own advertisements in the same corpus.

claims.notes: THE NEWSPAPER'S OWN BUILDING, ON A CORNER. The Democrat prints its imprint every week and it is an address: the building on the corner of South Water and Clark streets. That is a documented storefront for the one business whose existence the whole of this corpus depends on, and it is the earliest corner placement this reading pass has. It stands unchanged eight months later — the imprint of 1834-08-06 reads 'corner of South Water and' at the same point in the same setting — so the office did not move inside 1834. Two other businesses are advertised at this same corner in January (W. Kimball's New Store, 1834-01-21 and 1834-01-28), which says the corner carried more than one address.

claims.notes: MAIN STREET, NAMED, IN JANUARY 1834 — and that is why this claim is kept, because no street of that name survives in the town this project reconstructs. Either the Democrat's advertisers used 'Main-street' for a street the plat calls something else, or the OCR has taken a different name for it; nothing in this issue settles which, and the reading does not choose. THE ANCHOR IS THE USABLE PART: 'nearly opposite Graves' Tavern', the second business in this issue to place itself against a named public house (see claim c007), and the same Graves at whose house the Board of Trustees met a month earlier (claim c001). The advertisement is dated 26 November 1833 and is still running in January, and it runs again on 1834-01-14 (page 4) and 1834-01-21.

'East end of South Water-street' is a `street_only` placement with a direction, which is more than most of this corpus gives: it puts Cohen's store at the river-mouth end of the town's principal street, near Fort Dearborn rather than near the forks. Cohen's Store' (1834-01-28, claim c008 there) — so the store was well enough known to give an address against.

claims.notes: A SCHOOL BUILDING ON A NAMED CORNER: the Chicago Academy, at the corner of Water and Franklin streets, advertising in January 1834 as a going institution with a primary and a high English department, a book list and a charge for room and fuel. THE CORNER IS THE CLAIM. 'ER OF WATER AND F' is the tail of a standing head set in capitals, and 'F' is read Franklin because Franklin is the cross street the same column names elsewhere in this issue (G. Spring's office, 'the corner of Franklin and South Water-streets'); the supply is bracketed and the alternative — that 'Water' here is North Water rather than South Water — is NOT excluded by anything printed. The preceptor's name survives only as 'OAT, Preceptor.' in the interleaved line 1249 and as 'T. SPR' at line 1143, and is not supplied. For the reconstruction this is an institution that has to stand somewhere in 1835 and now has an 1834 address.

claims.notes: A TAVERN ON THE OTTAWA ROAD, THIRTEEN MILES SOUTH — which is a fact about the road network rather than about the town. It fixes that the route south-west toward Ottawa was travelled enough in the winter of 1833-34 to carry a public house at a day's short stage out, and it names the creek it stood on. The same advertisement runs unchanged in every issue of the month (1834-01-28, page 4 column 4, line 1175) and again in August 1834, so it is a standing insertion of about eight months.

claims.notes: A MANUFACTORY, NOT A STORE, AND IT BUYS ITS RAW MATERIAL IN THE TOWN. Elston & Co. make soap and candles and pay cash for tallow in any quantity and for good house ashes — ashes being the source of the lye, which is why a soap works and a town's hearths are economically joined. For a reconstruction this is a works with a rendering smell and a yard, and it is the earliest documented manufacturing in this reading pass after the saw-mill. It is still advertising in August 1834 (1834-08-06, page 4 column 1), so it survives the year. No site is given in this printing and none is inferred.
